name: Kryptos
title: The CIA Courtyard Code That’s Defeated Cryptographers for Decades
claims: Kryptos is a sculpture by Jim Sanborn located at the CIA headquarters in Langley, Virginia | 1
The sculpture was dedicated on November 3, 1990 | 1
There are four encrypted messages on Kryptos, most using a Vigenère cipher with a keyed alphabet using the keyword "KRYPTOS" | 1
The first three messages have been solved, while the fourth remains unsolved | 1
Jim Sanborn hinted a fifth coded message will reveal itself after the first four are solved | 1
The sculpture comprises four large copper plates with water, wood, plants, red and green granite, white quartz, and petrified wood | 1
The most prominent feature is a large vertical S-shaped copper screen resembling a scroll or computer printer paper | 1
Encrypted text is located in the northwest corner of the New Headquarters Building courtyard, outside the agency's cafeteria | 1
Characters are found within the 26 letters of the Latin alphabet plus four question marks, cut out of copper plates | 1
Sanborn placed other art pieces on CIA grounds, including granite slabs with sandwiched copper sheets and Morse code messages | 1
One stone slab has an engraving of a compass rose pointing to a lodestone | 1
The ciphers' increasing complexity through the entrance into the courtyard is intended to be like a fossil | 1
Other elements include a landscaped garden, fish pond with opposing wooden benches, reflecting pool, and a triangle-shaped black stone slab | 1
The name Kryptos comes from the ancient Greek word for "hidden", and the theme is "intelligence gathering" | 1
The cost of building the sculpture in 1988 was $250,000 | 1
The ciphertext on the left-hand side contains 869 characters in total: 865 letters and 4 question marks | 1
In April 2006, Sanborn stated a letter was omitted from the left side for aesthetic reasons to keep it visually balanced | 1
There are three misspelled words in the plaintext of the first three passages, which Sanborn claimed was intentional | 1
Three letters ("YAR") near the beginning of the bottom half of the left side are in superscript | 1
The right-hand side comprises a keyed Vigenère encryption tableau of 867 letters | 1
One line of the Vigenère tableau has an extra character (L), suggesting a reference to the Hill cipher | 1
Sanborn omitted the extra letter from small Kryptos models he sold | 1
Sanborn worked with retiring CIA employee Edward Scheidt to come up with the cryptographic systems | 1
Edward Scheidt stated the difficulty of the encryption was around nine out of ten and intended for it to be solved in five to ten years | 1
Scheidt noted an intentional change in the methodology of the encryption | 1
Sanborn suggested in 2005 that if he died before it was deciphered, he had a method to confirm a correct solution | 1
In 2020, Sanborn stated he planned to put the secret up for auction once he died | 1
In August 2025, Sanborn announced the K4 solution, prototype sculpture, encryption tables, and ephemera would be auctioned by RR Auction | 1
In October 2025, the auction was posted as part of "Decoding History: Kryptos, Enigma and the Rosetta Stone" from October 16 to November 20, 2025 | 1
A signed first-edition set of Howard Carter’s The Tomb of Tut-ankh-Amen was listed in the same collection | 1
Sanborn stated the sculpture contains a riddle within a riddle solvable only after the four passages are deciphered | 1
Sanborn gave conflicting information about giving the complete solution to CIA Director William Webster at the dedication | 1
A plaintext passage of the second message reads, "Who knows the exact location? Only WW." | 1
Jim Gillogly, a computer scientist from California, first publicly announced he solved the first three passages in 1999 using a computer | 1
CIA analyst David Stein solved the same passages in 1998 using pencil and paper, though it was only disseminated within the intelligence community at the time | 1
In November 1998, it was revealed a CIA analyst working on his own time had solved the lion's share of it | 1
An NSA team led by Ken Miller, along with Dennis McDaniels and two others, solved passages 1-3 in late 1992 | 1
In 2013, the NSA released documents under FOIA showing attempts to solve the puzzle in 1992 following a challenge by Bill Studeman | 1
By June 1993, a small group of NSA cryptanalysts had solved the first three passages | 1
Previous attempts found passage 2 ended with "WESTIDBYROWS", but in 2005 Nicole Friedrich determined "WESTXLAYERTWO" was possible | 1
On April 19, 2006, Sanborn informed an online community he omitted an S in ciphertext, confirming the plaintext ended with "WESTXLAYERTWO" | 1
Passage 1 method was Vigenère with keyword "PALIMPSEST" | 1
Passage 1 plaintext: BETWEEN SUBTLE SHADING AND THE ABSENCE OF LIGHT LIES THE NUANCE OF IQLUSION | 1
The word IQLUSION was claimed to be an intentional misspelling by Sanborn | 1
Keywords PALIMPSEST and ABSCISSA anagram into "P.S. It's as simple as ABC." | 1
Passage 2 method was Vigenère with keyword "ABSCISSA" | 1
Passage 2 plaintext includes coordinates 38°57′6.5″N 77°8′44″W, indicating a point about 174 feet southeast of the sculpture | 1
Passage 3 method was transposition | 1
Passage 3 plaintext is a paraphrased quotation from Howard Carter's account of opening Tutankhamun's tomb | 1
In November 2010, Sanborn released a clue that ciphertext "NYPVTT" becomes "BERLIN" | 1
In November 2014, Sanborn gave a clue to The New York Times that ciphertext "MZFPK" becomes "CLOCK" | 1
Sanborn stated solvers should delve into that particular clock, and in 2025 confirmed it referred to the World Clock | 1
In January 2020, Sanborn gave a clue that ciphertext "QQPRNGKSS" at positions 26 to 34 is "NORTHEAST" | 1
In August 2020, Sanborn revealed ciphertext "FLRV" at positions 22 to 25 is "EAST" | 1
In August 2025, Sanborn announced plans to auction the K4 solution on his 80th birthday, hoping the buyer would keep it secret | 1
The auction by RR Auction was expected to fetch between $300,000 and $500,000 | 1
